newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls response to juice-linked food poisoning.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls response to juice-linked food poisoning.

text.p: New cases of bacterial poisoning linked to apple juice were reported on Friday as a U.S. government agency said it was in talks with the juice industry about how to respond to the problem.

Health officials in Washington state, Colorado, California and Canada have reported more than 20 cases of a potentially lethal strain of E. coli bacteria that may be linked to unpasteurized apple juice made by the trendy California company Odwalla Inc.
In the wake of the outbreak, questions were raised in the media about the safety of unpasteurized fruit juices and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it was concerned.

"This is the first big producer shipping to many states where this sort of problem has come up. It does give us concern and we are discussing with the industry how to approach the problem," FDA spokesman Arthur Whitmore said.

The discussions could lead to new guidelines for handling fresh juice but it is too soon to say whether the FDA can order juice producers to pasteurize their product, he said. Pasteurization involves heating a liquid to kill bacteria.
Odwalla prides itself on the freshness of its juices, which contain no preservatives and are not pasteurized. The perishable juices must be processed, distributed and sold within two weeks.

Odwalla moved quickly in response to the outbreak, pulling many of its products from store shelves in its distribution region, which covers seven Western states and British Columbia. It has recalled 13 apple-juice-based products plus three other kinds of juice made on the same production line.
"Right now our deepest concern is for the health and safety of our customers and for anyone in the public," Greg Steltenpohl, chairman and co-founder of the 16-year-old company, said on Thursday.
The E. coli microbe normally lives in cattle but can be transmitted to humans through manure or improper slaughtering and can cause brain damage or death, especially in young children.
Two new cases of E. coli poisoning were reported in the Seattle area, bringing the total number of people stricken with the infection in Washington state since last week to 15.
A 22-year-old woman and an 8-year-old girl both became sick after drinking Odwalla juice, Seattle-King County health officials said. Neither has been hospitalized.

All but one of the 13 other people affected had drunk Odwalla drinks, the officials said. One of those affected, a child from Chicago, drank the juice while visiting Washington state and became ill after returning home.

Colorado health officials said four cases of E. coli sickness in the state probably were linked to Odwalla juice products and four more were being investigated. State health officials in California said they were investigating four cases of illness possibly linked to Odwalla apple juice.
In British Columbia, officials said they suspected three cases of the illness -- all affecting 3-year-old children -- were linked to the tainted juice.

U.S. and California officials were investigating the cause of the outbreak on Friday but had not yet reached any conclusions. Specialists from the FDA and the California Department of Health Services inspected Odwalla's manufacturing plant in Dinuba, California, and took many samples for analysis.

Odwalla said it was continuing efforts to retrieve potentially affected apple juice. It is also investigating the possible links between its products and the E. coli infections and cooperating fully with the FDA investigation, it said.
Odwalla stock, which plunged by about one-third on Thursday, steadied on Friday, rising $0.875 to $13 in Nasdaq trading.
